signals.title: @DavidLinthicum: The SaaS Resiliency Bill Is Coming Due We chose SaaS for good reasons: faster deployment, automatic updates, centralized controls, collabora
signals.content: The SaaS Resiliency Bill Is Coming Due We chose SaaS for good reasons: faster deployment, automatic updates, centralized controls, collaboration, and the ability to stop operating infrastructure that does not differentiate the business. But convenience is not resilience. Too many enterprise applications now depend on cloud back ends for identity, licensing, configuration, file access, synchronization, security policy, AI features, and core workflows. When one of those dependencies fails, software that appears local can become unusable—and an outage at a provider becomes a business interruption. The real issue is not whether cloud services are valuable. They are. The issue is whether we have mapped the dependencies that can stop critical business processes when a provider is unavailable. Redundancy at the component level does not automatically create resilience at the business-process level. A highly available cloud platform, network, and application can still leave the enterprise with a single, unmodeled point of failure. Architects need to move dependency risk from an invisible assumption to a design requirement. Know which services are mission-critical, define viable degraded modes, test operational workarounds, and ensure that uptime metrics are not substituting for real business continuity. Read more: https://t.co/qFCTgYSygr [1]

MergePulse AI is a commercial platform that aggregates pull‑request data from multiple code‑hosting providers into a unified command center. Securing U.S. satellite leadership requires effective diplomacy before and during the 2027 World Radiocommunication Conference in Shanghai, write @CSIS_Tech experts @TMTPolicyWonk and Stephan Lang. Read: https://t.co/oV9HdLOzoS
signals.score_reason: Twitter/X discussion signal. Final score: 40. Freshness: source age 0.96d.
signals.brief_en:
Title: @CSIS: China’s reusable‑rocket success and planned massive LEO satellite constellations challenge U.S. dominance. 
Brief: China has demonstrated a reusable launch vehicle and is advancing large‑scale low‑Earth‑orbit (LEO) satellite networks, narrowing the gap with U.S. space capabilities. To preserve U.S. leadership, Washington must engage in proactive diplomatic outreach ahead of, and during, the 2027 World Radiocommunication Conference in Shanghai, securing favorable spectrum allocations and international norms. The effort should combine technical coordination, alliance building, and transparent policy messaging to mitigate strategic surprise while acknowledging uncertainties about China’s timeline and commercial viability.

Unidentified MQ-25-like UAV: A mysterious aircraft resembling the US Navy's MQ-25 Stingray, measuring approximately 20.1 m in wingspan and 14.9 m in length. Its purpose remains unknown, with aerial refueling, reconnaissance and combat among the possible roles. CH-7: A large stealth flying-wing UAV developed for low-observable reconnaissance and potential strike operations. Jiutian: A heavy jet-powered unmanned aircraft designed to potentially serve as an airborne drone mothership, capable of deploying multiple smaller UAVs. The imagery highlights China's expanding development of advanced unmanned aircraft and suggests Pucheng may be an important flight-testing facility.
